text.what: A head, cast or carved, with a hole or a loop through the top for a cord. The face is the point: gazelle horns, human ears, a dog's muzzle, bulging eyes, wrinkled cheeks. Terracotta is the common material; bronze, iron, gold, glass and bone examples survive too. Some heads were fixed to cylinder seals or worn as brooches; larger stone versions hung on a wall. The full figure, where it appears, has a scaled canine body, two pairs of wings, a scorpion's tail, bird talons, right hand up and left hand down.
text.story:
Pazuzu is a demon employed as a doorman. He is the south-western wind, he carries plague, and the texts that address him call him "Agony of Mankind" and tell him to stay out of the house — and the same culture hung his face over the bed. In the bilingual Compendia he introduces himself: "I am Pazuzu, son of Ḫanbu, king of the evil lilû-demons. I was enraged (in violent motion) against the strong mountains and ascended them."

What he is for is Lamashtu. She snatches babies; he forces her back to the underworld. Ritual texts from Uruk direct that a woman be given a bronze Pazuzu necklace so that Lamashtu cannot make her miscarry; a Late Babylonian incantation against Lamashtu tells the reader to make a Pazuzu necklace and hang it round the afflicted person's neck; an Assyrian ritual text prescribes a Pazuzu head to banish sickness. Franz Wiggermann dates the figure's sudden appearance to the Early Iron Age, with the first images in the eighth century BCE from the tombs at Nimrud, the first texts in the seventh, the bulk of the finds in the seventh and sixth, and the latest under the Seleucids.

One of the large wall amulets was found where it fell. At Dur-Katlimmu, a Neo-Assyrian town, it lay on the floor of the main reception room, facing the entryway it had been hung to watch.

*Inference —* the heads are uniform and there are a great many of them. Eckart Frahm's study finds the appearance barely changes across his history. An object that looks the same everywhere and turns up everywhere was made in quantity by people who were not improvising, which is what the cited scholarship means when it calls the representations mass-produced.

dating.label: 8th century BCE to the Seleucid period
dating.note: First visual depictions in the 8th century BCE at Nimrud, first texts in the 7th, most representations 7th–6th, the most recent finds dating to the Seleucid Empire.

object.made_by: made in quantity and to a near-uniform pattern; the cited scholarship calls the heads, amulets and statues mass-produced

object.note: Heads have been found in graves as well as houses. No published measurement was read, so none is given.
